name: Victor Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, 27, and I run the electrical work on a small firm's repair jobs. I've a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, but the pay here is near the bottom and I have less than a month's expenses saved. I live with my partner Elise, we have no children, and there are few other electrical employers nearby. I label cables in pencil, test everything twice, and do my estimates on the same paper pad I've always used; I don't use AI, and arguing about new office software wears me out more than pulling cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads at the shop that I'd rather hear about tomorrow's jobs than another miracle app. I'll use the test kit that works and keep my records readable. If the office saves five minutes, fine, but leave the site work sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job itself seems steady in that picture, but our cash doesn't. Elise and I are one big van repair away from borrowing, and I can't walk into another firm down the street. I'm not calm just because the machines disappoint somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd cancel my weekend sports subscription and put that 15 toward the grocery bill each month. Through the next year I'd keep taking the same repair shifts and doing the test sheets by hand. I wouldn't borrow for a new device when the old pad does the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's an anxious sort of ordinary, if that makes sense. I don't expect an AI announcement to sack me, but I still listen hard when the van starts badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and your partner divide the bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elise does part-time stock work at a furniture shop, and the hours vary. We pay the rent first and work out food and travel after that. I'm not treating my partner's pay as money that can suddenly replace mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you accept a change to your records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my manager to show me an actual mistake in the paper sheets before replacing them. If there's a safety problem, of course it needs fixing. Buying something because the office is bored isn't a safety problem.

say: I'd ask colleagues to focus on **tomorrow's jobs**, rather than another promised miracle app.
I'd keep **test records** clear and accept useful office savings without changing site work blindly.
think: Our **cash is fragile** even if the electrical job carries on much as before.
A van repair could force **borrowing**, and few nearby employers offer another route.
do: Cancel the **sports subscription** now to free 15 monthly for groceries.
Keep taking **repair shifts** and completing paper test sheets through the next year.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, rather than expecting AI itself to remove his job.
S0.quote: I'm not calm just because the machines disappoint somebody.
fieldNote: He treats **financial insecurity** as separate from technological novelty and does not assume his partner can replace his income.
His resistance centres on **proven tools** and avoidable purchases, while leaving room to correct a demonstrated safety defect.

steps.text: Cancel the sports subscription to free 15 monthly for groceries
Keep electrical repair shifts and handwritten test sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the software can book a repair, but somebody still has to open the damaged socket. I wouldn't boast that electricians are untouchable. I'd ask the manager whether a faster booking desk means the same paid hours for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on work gives me some distance from the first changes. Still, if faster estimates turn every job into a tighter time allowance, my overtime could go. Losing even that bit of pay would hurt us, and I don't have much appetite for learning the new program at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the manager for the next month's booked hours in writing before agreeing to extra jobs. In the first year I'd cut the sports subscription as before and stop the weekly takeaway too, freeing another 10 a week. I'd keep my repair work and paper fault notes rather than start using AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious and a little cornered. Everyone says there's time to adjust, but that time often seems to mean my evening without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a new estimate allows too little time for a repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be shown the changed allowance on a real job. If it can't cover isolation, testing and putting the socket back safely, I'd record the extra time. I wouldn't sign a test I hadn't done just to make a screen happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training in the new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read a printed change to the booking procedure with my manager, but I wouldn't volunteer to try the AI tool. I learn best when I can see a finished, reliable method. At the moment I'd want the office to handle the office software.

say: I'd say **hands-on repairs** still need workers, without claiming the whole trade is protected.
I'd ask whether faster **booking** preserves our paid hours before praising the change.
think: My physical work delays the first impact, but tighter estimates could remove **overtime income**.
I dislike being expected to learn an unproven program during **unpaid evenings**.
do: Request **booked hours** in writing now before accepting extra jobs.
Cancel the subscription and **weekly takeaway** during the first year.
Continue **repair work** with paper fault notes instead of adopting AI.
feel: **Anxious and cornered** by possible lost overtime and pressure to adapt without pay.
S1.quote: I wouldn't sign a test I hadn't done just to make a screen happy.
fieldNote: He acknowledges **income exposure** through estimates while distinguishing it from immediate physical replacement.
Reading a printed procedure is **not AI adoption**; his explicit plan retains familiar tools and reduces spending.

steps.text: Cancel the subscription and weekly takeaway to reduce household costs
Keep electrical repair work with paper fault notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work that I want dates and booked jobs, not a speech about everyone becoming a computer expert. The thinking part comes in 2028, and the robot part around 2031. Those are different problems, even if both end up in my pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big part of my income to disappear once capable robots start doing the repairs around 2031. Before then the office changes could cut overtime, and I haven't the spare cash to wait through either loss. I lie awake doing the rent sums in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd stop the takeaway and subscription and speak to Elise about the rent if my hours fall. In 2029, after thinking AGI arrives, I'd ask my brother whether we could stay in his spare room for three months if wages drop sharply. I'd keep working while there are paid repairs; I wouldn't sign up for a course I don't understand and can't fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, with a plan that's smaller than the problem. I don't want a robot fight or a grand political argument. I want to know where our bed and tools would go if the rent can't be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask your brother for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother hasn't offered the room, so the first thing is to ask, not book a van. We'd offer money toward food if we had it and agree an end date. If the answer is no, I'd need to ask a local advice service about emergency housing; I don't know what we'd qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you ask for support before trying a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it sounds stubborn, but two years of panic wouldn't make me good at a screen job. I'd rather ask for help with actual bills than pay for a certificate because I'm frightened. I might need advice on learning later, but I wouldn't promise enrolment now.

say: I'd request **dates and booked jobs** instead of vague promises about becoming computer experts.
I'd distinguish **2028 office changes** from capable repair robots around 2031.
think: I expect **major income loss** when capable robots arrive, with earlier overtime cuts also possible.
My **thin savings** cannot absorb either gap, and the rent sums keep me awake.
do: Stop the **takeaway and subscription** now to reduce bills.
Ask my brother in **2029** about three months' accommodation if wages drop sharply.
Keep accepting **paid repairs** while work remains.
feel: **Alarmed about rent**, with limited plans and a clear awareness that family help is unconfirmed.
S2.quote: I want to know where our bed and tools would go if the rent can't be paid.
fieldNote: His **housing request** is conditional and unconfirmed; the transcript does not establish a move or an entitlement.
He rejects unfunded **course enrolment**, consistent with his risk aversion rather than a hidden retraining plan.

steps.text: Cancel the weekly takeaway and sports subscription now
Ask his brother about temporary housing in 2029 if wages fall
Continue accepting paid electrical repairs while work remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is better than two if the boss actually tells us what's being ordered. I'd want a yearly conversation about the booked work. I still wouldn't tell friends that another certificate guarantees a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have longer to put something aside before thinking AGI in 2031 and robots around 2034. I still expect a big income hit when the robots do ordinary repairs, so I'm not easy about it. The longer warning gives me a little more choice about the rent, not faith in a whole new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd set up a transfer of 10 each paid week into a separate account, using the takeaway saving. I'd keep doing repairs and ask for that yearly work review. During 2032 I'd take our actual wage records to a free household advice appointment and ask what help might exist if the later robot work cuts our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still alarmed about losing a big share of the wage. I can picture a better account balance by then, but I can't promise five years without a van bill. A plan feels useful without making me peaceful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an ordinary repair eats the money you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the van needs the money, I'd use the reserve to keep earning and restart the transfer after the repair. I wouldn't call that failure. My emergency savings account is there for real life, not to look impressive on a chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the yearly work discussion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the job diary, not just my fear. I'd ask whether the firm's bought machines or only watched a sales video, and whether next quarter's hours have changed. I can ask those questions without learning to use AI.

say: I'd say **five years** helps only if the firm shares actual equipment and work plans.
I'd avoid promising that an extra **certificate** guarantees another income.
think: I still expect a **large wage loss** when capable robots follow around 2034.
More warning improves my **rent options**, but doesn't turn me into an eager career changer.
do: Transfer **10 weekly** from takeaway savings when wages arrive, starting now.
Continue **repair shifts** and request an annual review of actual orders and hours.
Seek **free advice** in 2032 using wage records to check conditional support options.
feel: **Alarmed despite planning**, because expected losses remain large and savings could face ordinary emergencies.
S3.quote: My emergency savings account is there for real life, not to look impressive on a chart.
fieldNote: A longer runway improves **cash preparation** without erasing his expectation of major later earnings loss.
The advice appointment checks **eligibility**, while the saving plan explicitly allows interruption by essential van repairs.

steps.text: Save 10 per paid week from the cancelled takeaway
Keep repair shifts and request yearly orders-and-hours reviews
Take wage records to a free household advice appointment in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends that ten years is long enough to make a plan and also long enough for plans to change. I'll look at real work coming in each year. I won't pretend I enjoy the technology talk just because the date is farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 37 when the thinking machines arrive in 2036, so retirement doesn't solve anything. The immediate repair work seems safe enough, but I still need a wage after robots come around 2039. I can't see that far clearly, and the thin cushion means ordinary bills remain a worry now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the 10 weekly transfer now and keep it going when pay and van costs allow. Over the preparation years I'd ask annually about actual hours and robot orders, continuing repairs rather than buying speculative training. In 2037 I'd review the household budget with Elise and book free advice if our recorded hours are falling; I wouldn't assume help before checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious rather than lying awake about a definite near-term loss. The distance lets me think about next year's work without also packing a bag in my head. I still dislike depending on a wage I can't see beyond the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you discuss with your partner about the coming decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Elise we shouldn't promise a larger flat on the strength of years of overtime. We aren't planning children just now, and I wouldn't invent a family deadline because of a machine forecast. The useful conversation is about what rent we can afford on my basic hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your plan before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the order book stays full and the firm has bought nothing, I'd carry on and keep the annual check. If hours start falling earlier, I'd bring the advice appointment forward. Waiting for evidence isn't the same as forgetting to look.

say: I'd say **ten years** allows planning, while admitting that plans can change before the date.
I'd keep watching **actual work** instead of pretending enthusiasm for technology.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I will still need wages long after thinking AGI arrives.
Immediate repairs look fairly secure, but **ordinary bills** and later robot work keep me worried.
do: Start the **10 weekly** saving now when pay and essential van costs allow.
Continue **repairs** with annual checks of actual hours and equipment orders.
Review the budget in **2037** and seek free advice if recorded hours fall.
feel: **Anxious with breathing space**, because near-term job loss no longer feels definite.
S4.quote: Waiting for evidence isn't the same as forgetting to look.
fieldNote: The late date reduces **near-term distress**, but he correctly remains decades away from an assumed retirement solution.
He retains familiar work and uses **conditional advice**, rather than turning budget discussion into an unsupported family-plan action.

steps.text: Save 10 weekly when wages and essential van costs allow
Continue electrical repairs with annual hours and equipment checks
Seek free household advice in 2037 if recorded hours fall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the worst because the later robot date feels close before I've built any proper money. Written notice of changing hours would help more than a cheery meeting, and free advice that uses our real bills would help us plan. My tools fit in two boxes; our rent problem doesn't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You haven't asked what I mean by being slow to change. I can diagnose a burnt connection and teach a junior to test it safely; I just don't enjoy learning a new screen every month. I'd like people to remember those are different abilities.

headlineQuote: My tools fit in two boxes; our rent problem doesn't.
portrait: At **27**, Victor leads electrical repairs with a technical diploma and master licence, yet low pay leaves under one month's expenses.
He shares rent with **Elise**, his partner, has no children, and sees few alternative electrical employers nearby.
He avoids **AI tools**, trusts paper records, and asks practical questions about booked hours rather than choosing a political side.
Fast change prompts **housing enquiries** and spending cuts; longer warnings allow saving, while any advice or family help remains conditional.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to build cash before expected major earnings losses when capable robots follow.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** of changing hours and free advice grounded in actual household bills would make planning more useful.
